summary:
EcoShift lets a farmer test a crop rotation on their own fields before planting it. Farmers choose next year's crops months ahead, and a wrong choice only shows up at harvest.
So instead of guessing next year, EcoShift replays the last 44 real seasons (1982 to 2025) of NASA POWER daily weather on the farmer's own fields. You answer 13 short questions, and we fit a FAO-56 crop model to your spot with NASA POWER weather, USDA soils and your county's USDA harvests. Then we compare corn, soybeans, corn after corn, soybeans after soybeans, a cereal rye cover crop and oats, in bushels and in dollars (oats has no dollar figure), in a typical season and in the worst ones. On our example farm in Story County, Iowa, the current plan gets about 99% of a normal crop in a typical season and about 79% in a 2012-style drought.
Farmers can also drop in their real field boundaries. Each field gets its own NASA POWER weather and slope, and we check it from orbit with Copernicus Sentinel-2 field health, NASA fire detections, NASA soil wetness and live conditions, with any warning pinned to the exact spot on the field.
We built EcoShift as a multi-agent system: ten helpers, each with one job, pass their results along to the next. Six are plain code, like the crop model and the adviser that ranks the plans. Four use Google Gemini, for open chat questions, the outlook note, translation and reading the farmer's answers about their land, and our code checks everything they return.
details:
Project Details
What It Does And How It Works
Describe The Farm. The 13 questions ask where the farm is, what its four main fields grew last year, whether the land is owned or rented, how it handles water and drainage, what the budget and cost-share look like, what limits the farm, and what matters most to the farmer. Any question can be skipped, or you can load the example farm in one click. A 16-step guided tutorial walks through the simulator, with large text, keyboard controls and read-aloud.

Fit The Data To The Farm. We start with the daily weather of the nearest of 14 Corn Belt counties and shift it by the NASA POWER climate difference between that county and the farm. The soil comes from the USDA NRCS soil survey. The farm's normal harvest comes from USDA NASS yields for its own county. Outside the US we switch to ISRIC SoilGrids soils.

Replay 44 Seasons. The crop model grows each plan through every season from 1982 to 2025 using NASA POWER daily weather, one day at a time. It runs a FAO-56 soil-water balance and tracks growth stages with growing degree days. Planting waits until the field is workable, and the crop can lose yield to dry soil, waterlogging, frost and heat. Each plan finishes every season with a harvest and a dollar figure, based on Iowa State University crop budgets (again, no dollar figure for oats).

Compare And Decide. Every field gets a plain verdict, like "keep soybeans, worst season 88% of normal." Below it is a ranked list of options. Each one shows harvest and profit in a typical season and in the worst seasons, plus the evidence, the extra work involved and the information gaps. A 44-season strip shows the good and bad years at a glance. The farmer can change planting dates, irrigation, prices and the weather, or type a what-if into the chat, like "what if 2012 happens again?" On the example farm in Story County, Iowa, the current plan gets about 99% of a normal crop in a typical season. In a 2012-style drought it gets about 79%, a loss of about $37,200.

Import Real Fields. Upload a GeoJSON or KML file with up to four field outlines (from Google Earth, geojson.io or farm software), or use the built-in Iowa and California samples. Each field gets 44 seasons of NASA POWER weather for its own grid cell. Its slope and low spots come from the Copernicus GLO-30 elevation model, and it gets its own USDA soil and its county's normal yield.

Advanced Near-Real-Time Conditions. For imported fields we pull in many live layers. NASA VIIRS and MODIS fire detections come from NASA GIBS. NASA POWER root-zone and topsoil wetness is compared against the 2001 to 2025 normal. We also use ECMWF weather, Copernicus ERA5-Land soil moisture, CAMS air quality, ponds and wetlands from ESA WorldCover, and soil fertility from ISRIC SoilGrids. From Sentinel-2 we find bare soil, last summer's weak growth zones and possible burned ground. If NASA's fire satellites saw fire in the same place, the Sentinel-2 burn warning is marked confirmed. Warnings are numbered on a small map of the fields.

Field Health. We take a season of Sentinel-2 images (the clearest one in every 8 days) and build a time series for each field: NDVI, NDRE, NDMI, red-edge position, leaf area and uniformity. From that we get a health index and growth stage, scores for canopy, nitrogen, moisture, leaf structure and evenness, likely causes, and advice on irrigation, nutrition, soil moisture and uniformity. Phosphorus can't be seen from orbit, so for that the tool asks for a soil test.

30-Day Outlook. This is built on Open-Meteo's 16-day forecast and seasonal ensemble. It warns about frost, heat, dry spells and heavy rain.

Farm Map. The map is drawn from a USDA NAIP aerial photo or the Sentinel-2 cloudless map by EOX. Python and OpenCV turn the photo into an illustrated map and find the fields, which change colour as the season plays.

Languages. The simulator can be shown in Spanish, Portuguese, French, Hindi, Chinese, Arabic, Swahili, Vietnamese, Ukrainian or any other language you type in. Farmers can also type their questions in their own language.

How We Checked It
We tested the crop model against 44 years of USDA harvests, using Iowa corn and NASA POWER weather from Story County. Each season was scored with settings fitted without that season.

The model picks out the 1988 and 2012 droughts as two of its three worst seasons. Its error over all 44 seasons, about 10 points of a normal crop, is lower than the long-term yield trend's.

We also compared NASA Terra MODIS greenness over Story County with the real Story County corn harvests, and they track each other (correlation 0.61). Both the satellite and the model show the 2012 drought.

EcoShift supports the farmer's own judgment and local advisers. It does not replace them.

Benefits
A farmer sees how a rotation would have done in 44 real seasons, including the worst ones, before spending money on it, instead of guessing next year's weather.
Results come in bushels and dollars for their own fields, with a plain verdict for each field, and they can try a change on only part of a field by setting how many acres to test.
Real field outlines get satellite checks that are hard to piece together alone: field health through the season, weak spots, ponds and low spots, possible burned ground checked against NASA's fire satellites, and soil wetness compared with normal.
It is free, needs no account, runs in a phone's web browser and works in the farmer's own language.
Intended Impact
Farmers pick next year's rotation months ahead, going on habit and rules of thumb. Nobody knows the weather yet, and a wrong choice only shows up at harvest. In the 2012 drought, Iowa's corn harvest fell to about 77% of a normal year. With EcoShift, a farmer can see how a plan would have done across 44 real seasons, good and bad, on their own fields, before committing to it.

We want EcoShift to make it less risky to try rotations that build soil health, like breaking up corn after corn or adding a cereal rye cover crop, because the farmer can see the cost and the bad-year risk on their own fields first. After the hackathon we plan to test it with farmers and an extension office near us in California, add irrigated crops for California farms, and check more counties against their own USDA harvests before offering them.

Tools, Languages, Hardware And Software
Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS in the browser; Node.js on the server; Python for the farm map and the data scripts.
Libraries: none on the server side (Node.js built-in modules only); OpenCV, NumPy, SciPy and scikit-image in Python.
AI: the Google Gemini API, inside the app.
Hosting and testing: Vercel (the whole server runs as one function), GitHub, Node.js's built-in test runner for the 30 crop model tests, and Playwright for the browser tests, including 251 chat tests.
Hardware: none needed. EcoShift runs in a web browser on a laptop or a phone.
Every harvest and dollar figure comes from the crop model. The AI can only suggest changes from a fixed list, which the code checks, and a line under each chat answer shows which parts of EcoShift worked on it. The simulator also works offline with its built-in county data.

How It Is Creative
Instead of trying to predict next year, we flipped the question. Nobody knows next year's weather, but we do know the last 44 years, so EcoShift sends your plan back in time and plants it in every one of them. Your corn lives through the 1988 drought, the 2012 drought and 42 other real seasons on your own fields before you spend a dollar on it.

Your farm becomes a living map. We take a real aerial photo of a farm and turn it into an illustrated map with image processing, with no hand drawing. Then the crop model paints it week by week: you watch the fields come up green, turn gold and get harvested in any year since 1982.

You can ask it anything a farmer would. Type "what if 2012 happens again?" and the whole farm replays that drought in seconds, with the dollars it would cost. Under every answer, a line shows which of our helpers did the work. The AI can only suggest changes; our code checks them and the crop model does the math, so the numbers stay honest.

Two space agencies check each other. When Europe's Sentinel-2 satellite sees ground that looks burned, EcoShift asks NASA's fire satellites whether they saw a fire there. Only then is the warning marked confirmed.

We read the satellites ourselves. Instead of paying for an imagery service, our code pulls just the pixels over each field straight from the free Sentinel-2 archive, and decodes NASA's fire maps with an image reader we wrote. Drop in your field outlines from Google Earth, and in about 30 seconds each field has its own 44 years of NASA weather and its slope, with a full season of satellite health checks right after.

It speaks the farmer's language. The whole simulator, chat answers included, can switch to Spanish, Hindi, Swahili or any other language you type in, and farmers can ask their questions in that language too.

Factors We Considered
Farmers first: plain words, every question can be skipped, an example farm, and a 16-step guided tutorial with large text, keyboard controls, screen-reader support and read-aloud.
Phones and languages: it works on a phone, in 10 languages or any other the farmer types in.
Trust: every number comes from the crop model and public data, the AI cannot change the numbers, and we tested the model against 44 years of USDA harvests.
Privacy: answers are saved in the farmer's own browser, with no account and no advertising. Only the location and land answers go to public data services and the AI service, to fit the data to the farm.
Cost: EcoShift is free, every data source is public and free, and the AI helpers are optional.
Reliability: every outside data source has a time limit, so if one is slow the rest still shows.
Soil health and the challenge: it compares rotations and a cereal rye cover crop on each field's own soil, and it supports the farmer's own judgment and local advisers instead of replacing them.
Use Of AI
Claude (Anthropic) helped us write and debug the code, research the data sources and edit this text. Google Gemini runs inside EcoShift for the chat's open questions, the 30-day outlook note, translation and reading the farmer's answers about their land.
dataRefs: NASA POWER daily weather, 1982 to 2025 (every simulation)
NASA POWER climatology (fitting the weather to each farm)
NASA POWER soil wetness, MERRA-2 GWETROOT and GWETTOP (today's soil vs. normal)
NASA GMAO MERRA-2 reanalysis (temperature, rain, humidity and wind inside NASA POWER)
NASA CERES SYN1deg and GEWEX SRB sunlight (inside NASA POWER)
MODIS Terra NDVI 16-day 250 m (MOD13Q1, read through NASA GIBS; checks the model)
NASA VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20) and MODIS active fire detections (FIRMS, through NASA GIBS)
projectRefs: Copernicus Sentinel-2 Level-2A (ESA), via Element 84 Earth Search on AWS (field health, burned ground, weak zones)
Copernicus DEM GLO-30 (field slope and low spots)
Copernicus ERA5 and ERA5-Land (soil moisture, backup weather)
Open-Meteo (ECMWF forecast, seasonal, ERA5 and CAMS access)
Sentinel-2 cloudless 2020 by EOX (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) (farm map)
USDA NAIP aerial imagery via the USGS National Map (farm map)
USDA NRCS Soil Data Access (soil survey)
ISRIC SoilGrids (soils outside the US, soil fertility)
Iowa State Ag Decision Maker crop budgets
Photon geocoder by Komoot (worldwide address search)
Google Gemini API (chat, outlook note, translation, farm fit)
